Phase 1

Dataset Download and Import

This analysis is conducted in R using Bioconductor packages and other essential libraries for statistical and machine learning applications.

In this section, we will perform the following tasks: install and load the required packages, query and download gene expression data using the GDC data portal, and import the data into a suitable structure for downstream analysis.

Installation and Import of Packages

This section presents all the packages used in this work, which support data acquisition and analysis throughout the document, enhancing the efficiency of retrieving and interpreting relevant information. The code checks whether each package is already installed and installs it if necessary.

Data Query and Preparation

The GDCquery() function is used to perform a query on the database. In this function, several parameters are defined to filter the dataset that will later be downloaded.

The project parameter corresponds to the ID assigned to the cancer type, allowing the selection of information specifically related to endometrial carcinoma of the uterine body. The data.category parameter is used to specify the data category to be selected. In this case, since the goal is to perform transcriptomic analysis, the category “Transcriptome Profiling” was selected to retrieve gene expression profiling data.

Among the available gene expression profiling data, the analysis was restricted to gene expression quantification by setting data.type to “Gene Expression Quantification”. Finally, the desired type of gene expression analysis was specified, opting for “STAR-Counts”. This workflow indicates that the algorithm used to count gene expression from aligned sequences was based on the STAR tool.

The GDCdownload() function is then used to download the data according to the query defined in the previous step. Next, the GDCprepare() function was used to generate a SummarizedExperiment object, compiling all the downloaded data into a single object to facilitate further analysis. It is worth noting that this function also allows saving the data in .RData format, making it easier to reload using the load() function.

Note: This workflow enables the simultaneous download of both gene expression data and the associated metadata for the samples and genes.

# Define the base directory

# base_dir <- "/Users/mariacarvalho/Desktop/Mestrado/2º\ semestre/Extração"  # Change this to your desired path
# base_dir <- "/home/arog/Documents/university/2_semestre/ECDB/project_data"
base_dir <- "C:\\Users\\catar\\OneDrive\\Ambiente de Trabalho\\extracao\\projeto_r\\dadossss"


# Create directory if it doesn't exist
if (!dir.exists(base_dir)) {
  dir.create(base_dir, recursive = TRUE)
}

# File path for storing processed data
gdc_data <- file.path(base_dir, "GDCdata")
rna_seq_file <- file.path(base_dir, "mRNA_TCGA-LUAD.rda")

# Check if the data file already exists, if not, download and process
if (!file.exists(rna_seq_file)) {

  query_LUAD <- GDCquery(
    project = "TCGA-LUAD",
    data.category = "Transcriptome Profiling",
    data.type = "Gene Expression Quantification",
    workflow.type = "STAR - Counts"
  )

  GDCdownload(query = query_LUAD, directory = gdc_data)

  rna_seq_LUAD <- GDCprepare(
    query = query_LUAD,
    save = TRUE,
    save.filename = rna_seq_file,
    directory = gdc_data
  )

} else {
  rna_seq_LUAD <- get(load(rna_seq_file))
  rm(data)
}

Contextualization of the Data

Lung adenocarcinoma is the most common form of lung cancer and is classified as a subtype of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), representing about 40% of all lung cancer cases. It arises from the glandular cells of the lungs, which are responsible for producing mucus and lining the alveoli and other lung structures. This type of cancer typically develops in the outer, peripheral regions of the lungs and is known for its relatively slow growth compared to other lung cancer types [1][2]. Although there is a strong association with smoking, lung adenocarcinoma is also commonly found in non-smokers, particularly in younger women and individuals of Asian descent. It often emerges in areas of the lung affected by scarring or chronic inflammation. Early symptoms may be mild or vague, including fatigue, shortness of breath, or chest discomfort. As the disease advances, more pronounced signs can develop, such as a persistent cough, coughing up blood, and severe difficulty breathing [3][4]. The prognosis varies depending on the stage at diagnosis and response to treatment. Early detection improves survival rates significantly, while advanced cases may require multimodal therapies for disease management [2][4].

The TCGA-LUAD (The Cancer Genome Atlas - Lung Adenocarcinoma) project is part of the Genomic Data Commons (GDC), aimed at characterizing lung adenocarcinoma at the molecular level. It provides clinical, genomic, and molecular data, including patient demographics, tumor characteristics, sequencing data, and protein expression profiles.

Dataset Composition

The TCGA-LUAD collection encompasses 600 lung adenocarcinoma samples with extensive molecular profiling. The transcriptomic data captures expression levels for approximately 60,000 genes, providing unprecedented breadth in molecular characterization. Following rigorous quality control and preprocessing procedures, 27,326 genes were retained for downstream analysis, ensuring both data quality and comprehensive coverage of the transcriptome.

Research Focus

This study focuses on analyzing data and metadata to assess quality, completeness, and usability. By examining metadata, we evaluate its role in ensuring data consistency, accessibility, and interoperability for research applications.

Objectives

This project aims to: - Identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in LUAD - Investigate associations between gene expression and clinical variables - Discover biomarkers or gene signatures for prognosis or treatment

Research Applications

The richness and scale of this dataset make it an invaluable resource for: 1. Expression Profiling: Mapping transcriptional activity across the genome in lung adenocarcinoma 2. Molecular Subtyping: Classifying tumors into distinct biological and clinical entities 3. Pathway Analysis: Investigating dysregulated biological pathways driving LUAD development 4. Integrative Analysis: Combining transcriptomic data with other molecular layers and clinical information

Significance in Lung Cancer Research

The comprehensive nature of the TCGA-LUAD dataset supports efforts in understanding the molecular mechanisms driving lung adenocarcinoma and developing personalized therapeutic strategies. By integrating clinical variables with genomic data, this resource enables a multidimensional approach to investigating one of the most common and lethal cancer subtypes.

Data Pre-Processing

In this stage, we preprocess the dataset to ensure its quality for differential expression and enrichment analysis. First, we separate the gene expression data from the metadata, structuring the dataset for efficient analysis. Then, we apply filtering techniques to remove noise, retaining only biologically relevant information that will enhance the accuracy of downstream analyses.

# Extract gene expression matrix
expression_data <- as.data.frame(assay(rna_seq_LUAD))
expression_filtered <- expression_data[rowSums(expression_data > 1) > (0.5 * ncol(expression_data)), ]


# Extract clinical metadata
clinical_data <- colData(rna_seq_LUAD)

As a general rule in data preprocessing, variables with a high proportion of missing values can introduce bias or reduce the power of statistical analyses. Therefore, we chose to exclude variables with more than 30% missing values. This threshold strikes a balance between preserving as much data as possible while ensuring that the retained variables are informative and complete enough for meaningful analysis. By applying this filter, we focused the dataset on the most relevant and reliable features, which will improve the robustness of the downstream statistical and bioinformatic analyses.

# Set the NA threshold
threshold = 30  # in percent

# For clinical data
clinical_data_filtered = clinical_data[, percent_missing_clinical <= threshold]

columns_with_no_na <- names(clinical_data_filtered)[colSums(is.na(clinical_data_filtered)) == 0]

columns_with_no_na

Univariate Statistical Analysis

After filtering the variables, we selected the following as our feature variables: gender : Biological sex of the patient (Male or Female –> Categorical Variable). Can influence disease prevalence and progression.

# GENDER

barplot(table(clinical_data_filtered@listData[["gender"]]), 
        main = "Distribution of Gender", 
        xlab = "Gender", 
        ylab = "Count", 
        col = c("pink", "slategray1")[match(names(table(clinical_data_filtered@listData[["gender"]])), c("female", "male"))],
          border = "white")

race: Self-reported racial background of the patient (Asian, American indian or Alaska native, Black or African American, White, Not Reported, Unknown –> Categorical Variable). May reflect epidemiological or socio-demographic patterns.

# RACE

race_data <- clinical_data_filtered@listData[["race"]]
race_table <- table(race_data)


race_percent <- prop.table(race_table) * 100

race_df <- data.frame(
  Race = names(race_table),
  Count = as.vector(race_table),
  Percentage = round(as.vector(race_percent), 1)
)

print(race_df)

## 5                          Unknown     5        0.8
## 6                            white   466       77.7

Since the majority of patients are White (77.7%) or Black/African American (9.8%), and all other racial groups represent less than 2% each, we chose to focus our analysis on these two groups to ensure statistical relevance and interpretability.

Since the majority of cases are concentrated in Adenocarcinoma, NOS (56.19%) and Adenocarcinoma with mixed subtypes (14.48%), and the other tumor types each represent less than 1%, with the ‘Not Reported’ category also being excluded, we will focus our analysis on these two tumor types to ensure statistical relevance and improve the interpretability of the results.

# Keep only diagnoses with > 1% frequency
clinical_data_filtered <- clinical_data_filtered[
  clinical_data_filtered$primary_diagnosis %in% names(diagnosis_percent[diagnosis_percent > 1]), ]

# Remove "Not Reported"
clinical_data_filtered <- clinical_data_filtered[
  clinical_data_filtered$primary_diagnosis != "Not Reported", ]

table(clinical_data_filtered$primary_diagnosis)

## Bronchiolo-alveolar carcinoma, non-mucinous

# Set colors (1 per type)

colors <- c("#6A0572", "#9D0191", "#FF6464", "#FFAB73", "#FFC93C", "#F9F871")


# Plot
# Example of a pie chart
pie(
  table(clinical_data_filtered$primary_diagnosis),
  main = "Primary Diagnosis",
  col = colors,
  border = "white"
)

adjj_pathologic_stage: Represents the overall tumor stage (e.g., Stage I, II, III, IV) based on the AJCC (American Joint Committee on Cancer) system. This is a categorical clinical variable that reflects cancer progression and prognosis. It is highly relevant for survival analysis and differential expression studies, as advanced stages are typically associated with worse outcomes. Sub-stages denoted by letters such as A and B (e.g., IA vs IB) provide a finer classification within each stage, where A generally indicates a less advanced condition than B, often based on tumor size, lymph node involvement, or local invasion.

ggplot(clinical_data_filtered, aes(x = ajcc_pathologic_stage)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of AJCC Pathologic Stages",
    x = "AJCC Pathologic Stage",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

The bar plot shows the distribution of AJCC pathologic stages among patients in the dataset. The most common stages are Stage IA and Stage IB, which together represent the majority of cases. Higher stages such as Stage IIIA, IIIB, and IV are progressively less frequent, as expected in a cohort with a range of disease severities.

A small number of patients are labeled as simply “Stage I” without further sub-classification (e.g., IA or IB), and a notable number of samples have missing values (NA). To ensure consistency and analytical accuracy, these samples will be excluded from subsequent analyses.

tissue_type: Indicates the type of sample (Tumor, Normal –> Categorical Variable). Useful for distinguishing between diseased and control samples.

barplot(table(clinical_data_filtered$tissue_type),
        main = "Distribution of Tissue Type",
        xlab = "Tissue Type",
        ylab = "Count",
        col = c("forestgreen", "darkred"),
          border = "white")

The response variable chosen is: vital_status. Indicates whether the patient is Alive or Dead at follow-up (Categorical Variable). It has a binary classification target. For us it will be useful for survival outcome prediction.

barplot(table(clinical_data_filtered$vital_status),
        main = "Distribution of Vital Status",
        xlab = "Vital Status",
        ylab = "Count",
        col = c("plum", "plum4"),
          border = "white")

As previously described, we applied a gene filtering step to remove lowly expressed or non-informative genes. Specifically, we retained only those with counts greater than 1 in more than 50% of the samples. This early filtering step ensures that downstream analyses are performed on a high-quality, noise-reduced expression dataset.

Hypothesis Testing

As part of the exploratory analysis, hypothesis testing was conducted to evaluate potential associations between key clinical variables and patient outcomes. These tests aim to identify statistically significant differences between groups, guiding further investigation in downstream analyses. In this study, we focused on the variables vital status, gender, race, age at diagnosis, primary diagnosis, and AJCC pathologic stage. These variables were selected due to their biological relevance and potential impact on lung adenocarcinoma progression and prognosis.

Note: for all statistical tests performed below, a significance level of 0.05 was considered.

Vital Status by Primary Diagnosis

To explore potential differences in patient outcomes across histological subtypes of lung adenocarcinoma, we examined the distribution of vital status (Alive vs Dead) by primary diagnosis. The bar plot below displays the proportion of survival outcomes within each diagnosis group, highlighting subtype-specific survival patterns.

Among the subtypes, Adenocarcinoma (NOS) and Adenocarcinoma with mixed subtypes were the most represented. Notably, Adenocarcinoma, NOS showed a relatively higher proportion of deceased patients compared to some of the rarer subtypes, such as Acinar cell carcinoma and Mucinous adenocarcinoma, where survival rates appear higher.

However, the smaller sample sizes in certain groups (e.g., Mucinous and Papillary adenocarcinoma) limit the strength of direct comparisons. This variation underscores the importance of histological subtype in patient prognosis and suggests possible biological differences between subtypes.

A Chi-squared test was conducted to statistically evaluate the association between primary diagnosis and vital status. Although some subtypes show trends toward different outcomes, the test result (p = …) will help determine whether these observed differences are statistically significant.

chisq.test(table(clinical_df$vital_status, clinical_df$primary_diagnosis))
## 
##  Pearson's Chi-squared test
## 
## data:  table(clinical_df$vital_status, clinical_df$primary_diagnosis)
## X-squared = 8.2057, df = 5, p-value = 0.1453

The Chi-squared test is not reliable in this case, likely due to low expected counts in some cells. To address this limitation, we applied Fisher’s Exact Test with Monte Carlo simulation, which is more appropriate for contingency tables with small sample sizes or sparse data.

fisher.test(table(clinical_df$vital_status, clinical_df$primary_diagnosis), simulate.p.value = TRUE)
## 
##  Fisher's Exact Test for Count Data with simulated p-value (based on
##  2000 replicates)
## 
## data:  table(clinical_df$vital_status, clinical_df$primary_diagnosis)
## p-value = 0.1379
## alternative hypothesis: two.sided

Although there are visible differences in survival proportions across the primary diagnosis groups, the statistical tests did not find a significant association between vital status and primary diagnosis (p > 0.05 in both tests). This suggests that, within this dataset, histological subtype is not significantly associated with overall survival outcome — though sample size limitations, especially in rarer subtypes, may affect statistical power.

Vital Status by Gender

To investigate potential sex-based differences in patient outcomes, we analyzed the distribution of vital status (Alive vs Dead) across gender. The bar plot below displays the proportion of survival outcomes within each gender group, allowing for visual comparison of mortality rates between males and females. Understanding gender-related survival patterns can provide insights into biological differences, healthcare access disparities, or treatment responses that may influence prognosis in lung adenocarcinoma.

# Plot
ggplot(clinical_df, aes(x = gender, fill = vital_status)) +
geom_bar(position = "fill") +
geom_text(stat = "count", aes(label = ..count..), position = position_fill(vjust = 0.5), size = 3) +
labs(title = "Vital Status by Gender", y = "Proportion") +
theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
## Warning: The dot-dot notation (`..count..`) was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0.
## ℹ Please use `after_stat(count)` instead.
## This warning is displayed once every 8 hours.
## Call `lifecycle::last_lifecycle_warnings()` to see where this warning was
## generated.

The plot illustrates the proportion of patients who are alive or deceased within each gender group. Among females, 142 are alive and 65 are deceased, while among males, 94 are alive and 59 are deceased. Although the absolute number of female patients is higher, the proportional survival appears similar between genders.

No obvious survival advantage is visually evident for either gender in this sample. To determine whether these observed differences are statistically meaningful, a formal hypothesis test is required.

chisq.test(table(clinical_df$vital_status, clinical_df$gender))
## 
##  Pearson's Chi-squared test with Yates' continuity correction
## 
## data:  table(clinical_df$vital_status, clinical_df$gender)
## X-squared = 1.6934, df = 1, p-value = 0.1931

Since the p-value is greater than 0.05, we fail to reject the null hypothesis, indicating that there is no statistically significant association between gender and vital status in this dataset.

This confirms the visual impression from the bar plot: although there are slight numerical differences, the proportions of alive and deceased patients are statistically similar between males and females.

Vital Status by Race

To explore whether patient survival varies by racial background, we examined the distribution of vital status (Alive vs Dead) across different race categories. This allows for the identification of potential disparities in outcomes, which may reflect biological, environmental, or healthcare access differences.

The bar plot (not shown here) displays the proportion of survival outcomes within each racial group. While the proportions may vary slightly between groups, visual inspection alone is insufficient to confirm any meaningful pattern.

# Plot
ggplot(clinical_df, aes(x = race, fill = vital_status)) +
geom_bar(position = "fill") +
geom_text(stat = "count", aes(label = ..count..), position = position_fill(vjust = 0.5), size = 3) +
labs(title = "Vital Status by Race", y = "Proportion") +
theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

The bar plot displays the distribution of vital status (Alive vs Dead) across two racial groups: Black or African American and White. Among Black or African American patients, 33 were alive and 9 were deceased. In contrast, among White patients, 203 were alive and 115 were deceased.

Although the raw numbers differ due to sample size imbalance, the proportions of survival outcomes appear somewhat different between the groups when examined visually.

To formally assess whether these differences are statistically significant, a Chi-squared test should be applied. If the resulting p-value is greater than 0.05, we would conclude that there is no significant association between race and vital status in this dataset.

chisq.test(table(clinical_df$vital_status, clinical_df$race))
## 
##  Pearson's Chi-squared test with Yates' continuity correction
## 
## data:  table(clinical_df$vital_status, clinical_df$race)
## X-squared = 2.9446, df = 1, p-value = 0.08616

Since the p-value is greater than 0.05, we fail to reject the null hypothesis, indicating that there is no statistically significant association between race and vital status in this dataset. However, the p-value is close to the significance threshold, suggesting a possible trend that may warrant further investigation in larger or more balanced samples.

Vital Status by AJCC Pathologic Stage

To investigate the relationship between cancer severity and patient outcomes, we analyzed the distribution of vital status (Alive vs Dead) across different AJCC pathologic stages. As cancer stage is a key prognostic indicator, we expect higher stages to be associated with poorer survival.

# Plot
ggplot(clinical_df, aes(x = ajcc_pathologic_stage, fill = vital_status)) +
geom_bar(position = "fill") +
geom_text(stat = "count", aes(label = ..count..), position = position_fill(vjust = 0.5), size = 3) +
labs(title = "Vital Status by AJCC Pathologic Stage", y = "Proportion") +
theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

A clear trend emerges: earlier stages, such as Stage IA, show a higher proportion of patients alive (94 Alive vs 12 Dead), whereas advanced stages like Stage IIIB and Stage IV show a much higher proportion of deceased patients. For example, in Stage IIIB, only 6 patients are alive compared to 11 deceased — illustrating the sharp decline in survival as stage increases.

To statistically assess this relationship, both a Chi-squared test and Fisher’s Exact Test were applied:

chisq.test(table(clinical_df$vital_status, clinical_df$ajcc_pathologic_stage))
## 
##  Pearson's Chi-squared test
## 
## data:  table(clinical_df$vital_status, clinical_df$ajcc_pathologic_stage)
## X-squared = 49.065, df = 6, p-value = 7.235e-09
fisher.test(table(clinical_df$vital_status, clinical_df$ajcc_pathologic_stage), simulate.p.value = TRUE)
## 
##  Fisher's Exact Test for Count Data with simulated p-value (based on
##  2000 replicates)
## 
## data:  table(clinical_df$vital_status, clinical_df$ajcc_pathologic_stage)
## p-value = 0.0004998
## alternative hypothesis: two.sided

Both tests strongly reject the null hypothesis of independence (p < 0.001), confirming a significant association between AJCC pathologic stage and survival outcome. These results are consistent with clinical expectations: more advanced tumor stages are associated with significantly worse prognosis in lung adenocarcinoma.

Vital Status by Age at Diagnosis

To explore whether age at diagnosis influences patient survival, we compared the age distributions between patients who were alive and those who were deceased at the time of data collection. A boxplot was used to visualize potential differences in age between the two vital status groups.

ggplot(clinical_df, aes(x = vital_status, y = age_at_diagnosis , fill = vital_status)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = 21, outlier.fill = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Age at Diagnosis by Vital Status",
    x = "Vital Status",
    y = "Age at Diagnosis (years)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")  # optional: remove redundant legend

This visual trend suggests a possible relationship between age and survival, where older age at diagnosis may be linked to worse outcomes. However, the overlapping interquartile ranges also indicate that the difference may not be substantial.

# Shapiro-Wilk test for normality in each group
shapiro.test(clinical_df$age_at_diagnosis[clinical_df$vital_status == "Alive"])
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  clinical_df$age_at_diagnosis[clinical_df$vital_status == "Alive"]
## W = 0.98674, p-value = 0.02754
shapiro.test(clinical_df$age_at_diagnosis[clinical_df$vital_status == "Dead"])
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  clinical_df$age_at_diagnosis[clinical_df$vital_status == "Dead"]
## W = 0.96869, p-value = 0.005582

The Shapiro-Wilk test indicated that the age distributions for both the alive and deceased groups significantly deviate from a normal distribution (p < 0.05). To visually confirm this outcome, we generated Q-Q plots for each group, which further supported the presence of deviations from normality.

qqnorm(clinical_df$age_at_diagnosis[clinical_df$vital_status == "Alive"])
qqline(clinical_df$age_at_diagnosis[clinical_df$vital_status == "Alive"])

qqnorm(clinical_df$age_at_diagnosis[clinical_df$vital_status == "Dead"])
qqline(clinical_df$age_at_diagnosis[clinical_df$vital_status == "Dead"])

The plots show noticeable deviations from the diagonal line, particularly in the tails, further supporting the conclusion that the data are not normally distributed. Given the violation of normality assumptions, we proceeded with a non-parametric Wilcoxon rank-sum test to compare the age distributions between groups.

wilcox.test(age_at_diagnosis ~ vital_status, data = clinical_df)
## 
##  Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction
## 
## data:  age_at_diagnosis by vital_status
## W = 14714, p-value = 0.9304
## alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0

Since the p-value is much greater than 0.05, we fail to reject the null hypothesis, indicating that there is no statistically significant difference in age at diagnosis between patients who are alive and those who are deceased in this cohort.

Differential expression and enrichment analysis

Differential expression analysis

DESEQ2

In order to analyze the genes that are differentially expressed in the tumor type “Adenocarcinoma, NOS” within Lung Adenocarcinoma (TCGA, GDC), based on the patients’ vital status, a data pre-processing step was performed to facilitate and optimize the differential expression analysis while reducing computational time and resource usage.

clinical_df

Initially, samples with the primary diagnosis “Adenocarcinoma, NOS” were filtered, as only these samples are relevant to our study due to the higher incidence of this cancer subtype.

diagnosis_table

##                                           5 
##     Bronchiolo-alveolar adenocarcinoma, NOS 
##                                           3 
## Bronchiolo-alveolar carcinoma, non-mucinous

##                                           1 
##              Clear cell adenocarcinoma, NOS 
##                                           2 
##                        Clear cell carcinoma 
##                                           1 
##            Endometrioid adenocarcinoma, NOS 
##                                           1 
##             Granulosa cell tumor, malignant 
##                                           1 
##                       Hodgkin lymphoma, NOS 
##                                           1 
##            Infiltrating duct carcinoma, NOS 
##                                           1 
##           Invasive micropapillary carcinoma 
##                                           1 
##                    Medullary carcinoma, NOS 
##                                           1 
##                     Mucinous adenocarcinoma 
##                                          19 
##                                Not Reported 
##                                          45 
##               Papillary adenocarcinoma, NOS 
##                                          18 
##       Papillary transitional cell carcinoma 
##                                           1 
##                        Solid carcinoma, NOS 
##                                           4 
##                Squamous cell carcinoma, NOS 
##                                           4
metadata_col = SummarizedExperiment::colData(rna_seq_LUAD)
geneExp = SummarizedExperiment::assay(rna_seq_LUAD, "unstranded")
filtered_data <- metadata_col[!is.na(metadata_col$primary_diagnosis) &
                              metadata_col$primary_diagnosis == "Adenocarcinoma, NOS", ]
ADC_data <- geneExp[, rownames(filtered_data)]
expression_filtered = metadata_col[!is.na(metadata_col$primary_diagnosis),]
expression_filtered = expression_filtered[expression_filtered$primary_diagnosis=="Adenocarcinoma, NOS",]

After subsetting the dataset to include only samples with a primary diagnosis of “Adenocarcinoma, NOS”, the gene expression matrix (ADC_data) contained 60,660 genes. Since there were no missing values in the expression data, all annotated genes were initially retained. However, many of these genes either showed no expression or had consistently low expression across the samples, which can introduce noise in downstream analyses. To address this, an additional filtering step was applied to remove genes with zero counts across all samples, as well as those with fewer than 20 counts in fewer than 4 samples. These filtering criteria follow standard guidelines from the DESeq2 workflow, ensuring that only genes with sufficient expression are retained for meaningful differential expression analysis.

Next, we checked for missing values in the vital status column.

sum(is.na(expression_filtered$vital_status))
## [1] 0
expression_filtered$vital_status = factor(expression_filtered$vital_status)

Since no missing values were found, the “vital_status” metadata was converted into a factor, as the differential expression analysis using the DESeq2 package recommends using factors instead of character variables.

After the preprocessing steps, the final dataset included approximately 33,293 genes and 323 samples. With this filtered dataset, we created the DESeqDataSet object, using the “vital_status” factor as the explanatory variable in the model. This analysis used a significance threshold of α = 0.05 to identify genes differentially expressed between vital status groups.

ddsSE = DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(countData = ADC_data, colData = expression_filtered, design = ~vital_status)

keep_genes = rowSums(counts(ddsSE) >= 20) >= 4
ddsSE = ddsSE[keep_genes, ]
dim(ddsSE)
## [1] 33293   323

After the preprocessing steps, the final dataset included approximately 33,293 genes and 323 samples. With this filtered dataset, we created the DESeqDataSet object, using the “vital_status” factor as the explanatory variable in the model.

ddsSE_norm = DESeq(ddsSE)
res = results(ddsSE_norm, alpha = 0.05)

summary(res) # summary of differential expression test results
## 
## out of 33293 with nonzero total read count
## adjusted p-value < 0.05
## LFC > 0 (up)       : 1496, 4.5%
## LFC < 0 (down)     : 4498, 14%
## outliers [1]       : 0, 0%
## low counts [2]     : 0, 0%
## (mean count < 0)
## [1] see 'cooksCutoff' argument of ?results
## [2] see 'independentFiltering' argument of ?results
sum(res$padj < 0.05, na.rm=TRUE) # Total number of genes with differential expression
## [1] 5994

Differential gene expression analysis was performed using DESeq2 on a dataset comprising 33,293 genes with non-zero read counts across 323 samples.

de_gene_count <- sum(res$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
print(de_gene_count)
## [1] 5994

Following model fitting and hypothesis testing, a total of 5,994 genes were found to be differentially expressed with an adjusted p-value below 0.05.

This analysis highlights a considerable shift in gene expression, particularly toward downregulation, which may reflect underlying biological processes or responses in the studied conditions.

# Total number of tested genes
total_genes <- sum(!is.na(res$padj))

# Number of significantly differentially expressed genes (padj < 0.05)
sig_genes <- sum(res$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)

# Percentage of DE genes
percent_DE <- round((sig_genes / total_genes) * 100, 2)

# Among DE genes, count upregulated and downregulated
upregulated <- sum(res$padj < 0.05 & res$log2FoldChange > 0, na.rm = TRUE)
downregulated <- sum(res$padj < 0.05 & res$log2FoldChange < 0, na.rm = TRUE)
## Total tested genes: 33293
## Significantly DE genes: 5994 ( 18 % )
## Upregulated: 1496
## Downregulated: 4498
#  graphical display of results
DESeq2::plotMA(res, main="DESeq2 differential expression analysis")

Differential expression analysis using DESeq2 identified 5,994 genes (approximately 18% of the 33,293 tested) as significantly differentially expressed between the “Alive” and “Dead” groups, based on an adjusted p-value (padj) threshold of < 0.05. Of these, 1,496 genes were significantly upregulated, while 4,498 genes were downregulated, indicating a strong bias toward decreased expression. This trend was further supported by the MA plot, which revealed a higher density of significantly downregulated genes with negative log2 fold changes. These findings suggest notable shifts in gene expression, potentially reflecting underlying biological mechanisms or regulatory changes associated with the studied condition.

plotCounts(ddsSE_norm, gene=which.min(res$padj), intgroup="vital_status", pch = 19)

plotCounts(ddsSE_norm, gene=which.min(res$padj), intgroup="vital_status", pch = 19)

resOrdered = res[order(res$padj),]
resOrdered[1,]
## log2 fold change (MLE): vital status Dead vs Alive 
## Wald test p-value: vital status Dead vs Alive 
## DataFrame with 1 row and 6 columns
##                    baseMean log2FoldChange     lfcSE      stat      pvalue
##                   <numeric>      <numeric> <numeric> <numeric>   <numeric>
## ENSG00000202538.1   111.563       -4.21026  0.394484  -10.6728 1.36399e-26
##                          padj
##                     <numeric>
## ENSG00000202538.1 4.54112e-22

ENSG00000202538.1 showed high expression in both groups but with reduced variability among “Dead” samples, possibly indicating more uniform gene regulation in that condition.

Together, these observations support the global trend identified in the analysis and highlight genes that may be biologically relevant in the context of survival.

edgeR

To mitigate biases introduced by differences in sequencing depth or library size, normalization of the raw count data was performed prior to downstream analyses such as differential expression testing. This step is critical to ensure meaningful biological comparisons between samples. The cpm() function is used to normalize raw count data (ADC_data) by converting it into Counts Per Million (CPM). This method adjusts for differences in library sizes across samples, making the data comparable.

# Normalization of count data
ADC_data_CPM <- cpm(ADC_data)
ADC_data_CPM_log <- cpm(ADC_data, log = TRUE)
dim(ADC_data_CPM)
## [1] 60660   323

The cpm() function from the edgeR package was used to convert raw counts in ADC_data into Counts Per Million (CPM). This normalization accounts for library size by scaling the raw counts relative to the total number of reads per sample, multiplied by one million. The resulting ADC_data_CPM matrix contains normalized expression values that are directly comparable across samples. The dim() function is then used to inspect the dimensions of the resulting CPM matrix, providing a quick check on the number of genes and samples retained after normalization.

To identify genes with meaningful levels of expression, a logical matrix min_exp is created. Each entry in this matrix evaluates whether a gene’s CPM value exceeds 0.5 in a given sample. The rowSums(min_exp) >= 2 condition ensures that only genes with a CPM value greater than 0.5 in at least two samples are retained for further analysis. This filter eliminates genes with minimal or no detectable expression across the dataset, which could otherwise introduce noise or bias into the analysis. The filtered dataset ADC_data_filtered thus contains only those genes deemed reliably expressed, enhancing the robustness and interpretability of subsequent steps.

# Removal of genes that do not have an expression of 0.5 or higher in at least 2 samples 
min_exp = ADC_data_CPM > 0.5
keep_rows =  rowSums(min_exp) >= 2
ADC_data_CPM_filt = ADC_data_CPM[keep_rows,]
dim(ADC_data_CPM_filt)
## [1] 37183   323
# Transformation of standardized counts
dgeObj = DGEList(ADC_data_CPM_filt)
log_geneExp_filt = cpm(dgeObj, log=TRUE)
boxplot(log_geneExp_filt[,1:100], xlab="", ylab="Log2 counts per million",las=2)
abline(h=median(log_geneExp_filt),col="deeppink")
title("Boxplots of logCPMs (not normalized)")

This boxplot confirms that there is variability in expression distributions across our samples, justifying normalization. It also supports our decision to apply a CPM > 0.5 filter in at least 2 samples, as many genes appear to hover near or below that threshold.

# Normalization of the library size of each sample
dgeObj = calcNormFactors(dgeObj)

After creating the DGEList object dgeObj containing raw count data, normalization factors are calculated using the calcNormFactors() function from the edgeR package. This step accounts for compositional differences between libraries that are not due to sequencing depth alone—such as the presence of a few highly expressed genes in some samples. The method scales the raw counts so that expression levels are comparable across samples, ensuring that observed differences reflect biological variation rather than technical artifacts.

To perform a differential expression analysis, a design matrix is constructed to specify the experimental conditions.

# Differential expression analysis
vital_status = as.factor(expression_filtered$vital_status)
design = model.matrix(~vital_status)

Here, vital_status (“Alive” vs. “Dead”) is extracted from the metadata and converted into a factor to indicate categorical grouping. The model.matrix() function then builds a design matrix based on this grouping, where the intercept represents one condition (the baseline), and the second column represents the contrast of interest.

# To estimate common dispersion, trend dispersion and tag dispersion in a single run
dgeObj = estimateDisp(dgeObj, design = design)

fit = glmFit(dgeObj, design)

lrt = glmLRT(fit, coef=2)
topTags(lrt)
## Coefficient:  vital_statusDead 
##                        logFC   logCPM       LR       PValue          FDR
## ENSG00000138379.5  -4.438296 2.782580 94.10201 2.996750e-22 1.114281e-17
## ENSG00000122585.8   5.927629 3.558316 91.69916 1.009079e-21 1.876029e-17
## ENSG00000122711.9  -5.349381 3.871353 81.53690 1.720196e-19 2.132069e-15
## ENSG00000130055.14  2.523746 1.400211 78.72808 7.127527e-19 5.319440e-15
## ENSG00000204941.14  5.137144 2.128855 78.72102 7.153054e-19 5.319440e-15
## ENSG00000140274.14  2.324817 2.101725 69.95399 6.070386e-17 3.761919e-13
## ENSG00000198788.9   3.876851 3.378918 67.30158 2.329950e-16 1.237636e-12
## ENSG00000145692.15 -3.464062 2.197283 66.84847 2.932001e-16 1.362758e-12
## ENSG00000261742.6  -2.691868 2.573328 66.14048 4.199023e-16 1.734803e-12
## ENSG00000160181.9   5.408794 4.833704 65.79694 4.998575e-16 1.858620e-12

estimateDisp() estimates three types of dispersion in one step:

Common dispersion: overall variability across genes.
Trend dispersion: dependence of dispersion on gene abundance.
Tagwise dispersion: gene-specific dispersion values.

glmFit() fits a negative binomial generalized linear model (GLM) to the count data using the provided design matrix. This model incorporates the estimated dispersions and allows for group-wise comparisons. glmLRT() performs a likelihood ratio test for differential expression. The coef = 2 argument specifies that the second column of the design matrix is the coefficient being tested. topTags(lrt) returns a ranked table of genes based on statistical significance, with adjusted p-values (FDR) and log-fold changes, highlighting the most differentially expressed genes between the two groups.

#Genes information (underexpressed (down), not significant(NotSig), overexpressed(Up))

summary(decideTests(lrt))
##        vital_statusDead
## Down               1004
## NotSig            34874
## Up                 1305
# Graphic visualization of differentially expressed genes
plotMD(lrt)
abline(h=c(-1, 1), col="burlywood2")

There is a much larger cluster of blue points below zero, indicating a strong downregulation trend in the “Dead” group. This aligns with our earlier stat showing 4,498 downregulated genes, compared to only 1,496 upregulated. The density of black points near the logFC = 0 line shows that the majority of genes are not differentially expressed, which is typical in RNA-seq datasets. The horizontal brown lines indicate a fold-change threshold. Genes beyond these lines have substantial expression shifts.

This plot supports the earlier conclusion that the “Dead” group shows a global downregulation pattern compared to the “Alive” group. This could suggest transcriptional repression or loss of cellular function associated with death or disease severity.

# glmTreat is used to filter the DE genes and focus only on the genes that are most biologically significant
# filter out the differentially expressed genes with the greatest biological importance

filtered_results = glmTreat(fit, lfc=log2(1.5))
topTags(filtered_results)

This version appears to show fewer significantly regulated genes, as seen by the smaller number of red and blue dots. Most points remain concentrated around the zero log-fold-change line, implying that most genes are not significantly different between the Alive and Dead groups. The few upregulated genes (red) cluster on the left side (lower expression), suggesting that significant changes may be occurring in lowly expressed genes. The downregulated genes (blue) also appear mostly in low-expression regions. While the trend of downregulation in the “Dead” group still exists, the number of differentially expressed genes is lower, suggesting that after stricter filtering the DE genes and focus only on the genes that are most biologically significant, only the most robust changes are retained.

Enrichment analysis

The goal of this section is to identify genes whose expression levels differ significantly between the two clinical conditions (“Alive” vs. “Dead”) and prepare the results for downstream enrichment analysis. We use a generalized linear model (GLM) approach implemented in the edgeR package to perform this task.

vital_status = as.factor(expression_filtered$vital_status)
design = model.matrix(~vital_status)

dgeObj = estimateDisp(dgeObj, design = design)


fit = glmFit(dgeObj, design)

lrt = glmLRT(fit, coef=2)
topTags(lrt)

Phase 2 - Unsupervised Analysis

1. Dimensionality Reduction

High-dimensional biological datasets, such as transcriptomic profiles, often contain thousands of variables per sample. This complexity can obscure meaningful biological patterns or relationships between samples.
To address this, we applied dimensionality reduction techniques that project high-dimensional data into a lower-dimensional space while preserving important global or local structures.

In this analysis, we used a combination of: - Principal Component Analysis (PCA), to identify the main axes of variation and reduce noise in the data, - t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE), which emphasizes local relationships and can reveal subtle clusters or subgroups, - and Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP), a recent method that balances the preservation of both global and local data structure and is computationally more efficient than t-SNE.

These methods complement each other: PCA provides a general overview of variance across the dataset, while t-SNE and UMAP allow for more refined visualization of local similarities and potential sample groupings. Together, they offer a robust approach to exploring underlying structures that may reflect biological or clinical relevance.

PCA (Principal Component Analysis)

pca_data = t(ADC_data_CPM_log)  # transpose: samples in columns, genes in rows


pcares1 <- prcomp(pca_data, scale = FALSE)  # data already normalized

In this dataset, consisting of 60,660 genes and 600 samples, it was determined that 253 principal components are required to explain at least 95% of the total variance. This reflects the effect of using log-transformed CPM values, which distributes variance more evenly across components and reduces the dominance of highly expressed genes. The variance plot demonstrates that the first two principal components capture only a modest portion of the total variability. Nevertheless, they are still useful for an initial low-dimensional visualization of the data structure, although deeper patterns are likely embedded in higher-order components.

# Clean PCA scatterplot (PC1 vs PC2)

pca_df <- as.data.frame(pcares1$x)
pca_df$sample_id <- rownames(pca_df)

ggplot(pca_df, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "darkblue", size = 2) +
  labs(title = "PCA Scatterplot: PC1 vs PC2", x = "PC1", y = "PC2") +
  theme_minimal()

The PCA scatterplot of the first two principal components, based on log-transformed CPM data, shows a dense cluster of samples with no evident subgroups or distinct separations. This indicates that PC1 and PC2 capture only limited structure within the dataset and are insufficient to visually distinguish biological or clinical subtypes.

Furthermore, the explained variance plot reveals that 253 components are required to account for at least 95% of the total variance, reflecting the high dimensionality and complexity of the transcriptomic data. This distribution suggests that meaningful biological patterns may be embedded in higher-order or nonlinear dimensions, motivating the use of alternative dimensionality reduction techniques such as t-SNE and UMAP.

PCA by Clinical Variables

To better investigate the potential biological or clinical groupings within the data, the PCA results were visualized with samples colored by key clinical features. These visualizations help assess whether specific sample groupings, observed in lower-dimensional space, correlate with clinical variables such as vital status, primary diagnosis, gender, race, AJCC stage, or age at diagnosis.

Although PCA is an unsupervised method and does not explicitly use class labels during its computation, overlaps or separations between sample groups in PCA plots may reveal biologically meaningful trends.

Interpretation of PCA by Clinical Variables

Visualizing the first two principal components after log-transformation, colored by clinical variables, confirms several key limitations of linear dimensionality reduction in this context:

  • No evidence of group separation: Across all visualizations (primary diagnosis, gender, race, AJCC stage, and age at diagnosis), samples form a dense cloud with extensive overlap between categories. PC1 and PC2 fail to separate any clinical or demographic group, highlighting the limited clinical interpretability of the first two PCs.

  • Severe class imbalance in primary diagnosis: Almost all samples are classified as Adenocarcinoma, NOS, which restricts variability and prevents meaningful comparisons for this variable.

  • AJCC stage and age show no clear alignment: While stages and age are continuous or ordinal variables, the plots show scattered distributions with no visible gradient or directional trend, suggesting no linear association with the main components.

  • Gender and race remain mixed: Samples from different genders and racial groups are completely interspersed, indicating that these demographic factors do not contribute to major axes of transcriptomic variance in the data.

  • Vital status does not explain variance: “Alive” and “Dead” samples overlap entirely, reinforcing that survival status is not captured by the dominant linear structure in the dataset.

Conclusion and Justification for Nonlinear Methods

These updated PCA results, using log-transformed data, further emphasize that linear projections fail to reveal meaningful clinical or biological structure. The lack of visible grouping supports the need for nonlinear dimensionality reduction techniques, which can capture relationships that do not lie along straight axes.

We therefore proceed with:

  • t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE): optimized to preserve local relationships and uncover subtle patterns.
  • Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP): better at preserving both global and local structure, while being faster and more stable for large datasets.

These methods are more suitable for revealing potentially nonlinear biological variation that may correspond to latent clinical subtypes.

t-SNE (t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding)

t-SNE is a non-linear dimensionality reduction technique that maps high-dimensional data to a low-dimensional space by preserving the probability distribution of pairwise similarities. It is particularly well-suited to reveal local clusters or subgroup patterns that PCA might miss due to its linear nature.

Before running t-SNE, we removed duplicate entries and used the PCA-reduced data as input, a common practice to reduce noise and improve computational efficiency.

# Store t-SNE coordinates
tsne_df <- as.data.frame(res_tsne$Y)
colnames(tsne_df) <- c("tSNE1", "tSNE2")
rownames(tsne_df) <- rownames(dados_CPM_nd)

clinical_df_filtered <- clinical_df[rownames(tsne_df), ]
tsne_df_final <- cbind(tsne_df, clinical_df_filtered)

Now, we visualize the t-SNE embeddings colored by clinical and demographic attributes:

# t-SNE by Vital Status and Gender
ggplot(tsne_df_final, aes(x = tSNE1, y = tSNE2, color = gender, shape = vital_status)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "t-SNE: Gender & Vital Status")

# t-SNE by Primary Diagnosis and Vital Status
ggplot(tsne_df_final, aes(x = tSNE1, y = tSNE2, color = primary_diagnosis, shape = vital_status)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "t-SNE: Primary Diagnosis & Vital Status")

# t-SNE by AJCC Stage and Vital Status
ggplot(tsne_df_final, aes(x = tSNE1, y = tSNE2, color = ajcc_pathologic_stage, shape = vital_status)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "t-SNE: AJCC Stage & Vital Status")

# t-SNE by Race and Vital Status
ggplot(tsne_df_final, aes(x = tSNE1, y = tSNE2, color = race, shape = vital_status)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "t-SNE: Race & Vital Status")

# t-SNE by Age and Vital Status
ggplot(tsne_df_final, aes(x = tSNE1, y = tSNE2, color = age_at_diagnosis, shape = vital_status)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_color_viridis_c() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "t-SNE: Age & Vital Status")

Interpretation of t-SNE by Clinical Variables

The t-SNE embeddings, computed from log-transformed data, reveal no clear separation between clinical or demographic groups. Samples remain largely intermixed across all variables, including gender, race, AJCC stage, age, and vital status.

While t-SNE exposes some local structure, these patterns do not align with any of the annotated clinical features, suggesting that other factors—possibly molecular or technical—drive the observed variation.

These results reinforce the conclusion that the clinical variables analyzed do not correspond to distinct transcriptomic profiles, even in a nonlinear embedding.

UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection)

UMAP is another powerful non-linear method that builds on manifold learning and topological data analysis. Compared to t-SNE, UMAP generally offers better global structure retention and can be tuned to emphasize either local or global features.

We applied UMAP using the same PCA-reduced input to maintain consistency and avoid redundancy in high-dimensional noise.

library(umap)

# Run UMAP
umap_res <- umap(dados_CPM_nd)
umap_df <- as.data.frame(umap_res$layout)
colnames(umap_df) <- c("UMAP1", "UMAP2")
clinical_df_filtered <- clinical_df[rownames(umap_df), ]  
umap_df <- cbind(umap_df, clinical_df_filtered)

And we visualize the UMAP projection:

# UMAP by Vital Status and Gender
ggplot(umap_df, aes(x = UMAP1, y = UMAP2, color = gender, shape = vital_status)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "UMAP: Gender & Vital Status")

# UMAP by AJCC Stage and Vital Status
ggplot(umap_df, aes(x = UMAP1, y = UMAP2, color = ajcc_pathologic_stage, shape = vital_status)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "UMAP: AJCC Stage & Vital Status")

# UMAP by Race and Vital Status
ggplot(umap_df, aes(x = UMAP1, y = UMAP2, color = race, shape = vital_status)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "UMAP: Race & Vital Status")

# UMAP by Age and Vital Status
ggplot(umap_df, aes(x = UMAP1, y = UMAP2, color = age_at_diagnosis, shape = vital_status)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_color_viridis_c() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "UMAP: Age & Vital Status")

Interpretation of UMAP by Clinical Variables

The UMAP projections reveal structured groupings in the transcriptomic space, with some visible clustering. However, these clusters do not align with any of the clinical or demographic variables considered — including gender, race, AJCC stage, age, or vital status.

This indicates that while UMAP captures meaningful relationships in the data, the observed structure is likely driven by latent biological or technical factors, rather than the available clinical annotations.

Final Remarks on UMAP

UMAP projections revealed more defined structures compared to PCA and t-SNE, with denser local groupings and clearer spatial organization. However, these structures did not correspond to the available clinical features, reinforcing the likelihood that other, unmeasured biological factors underlie the observed transcriptomic variation.

Clustering

Clustering is a type of unsupervised machine learning that finds hidden patterns in data by grouping similar items together. It uses distance or similarity measurements to form groups (clusters) so that items in the same group are as similar as possible, and items in different groups are as different as possible. In this analysis, we used two main clustering methods: 1. Hierarchical Clustering: builds a tree-like diagram (dendrogram) by repeatedly joining the closest items or groups without needing to set the number of clusters in advance. 2. K-means Clustering: splits the data into a fixed number (K) of groups by minimizing the distances between items and the center (centroid) of their group.

Before clustering, we converted the normalized gene expression data into a matrix format. Since the clustering methods need numerical matrices, this step ensures that the data can be processed. For sample-based analysis, we also transposed the matrix so that samples are in the rows and genes are in the columns.

# Normalize RNA-seq data using DESeq
ddsSE_normalized <- DESeq(ddsSE)
## estimating size factors
## estimating dispersions
## gene-wise dispersion estimates
## mean-dispersion relationship
## final dispersion estimates
## fitting model and testing
## -- replacing outliers and refitting for 8521 genes
## -- DESeq argument 'minReplicatesForReplace' = 7 
## -- original counts are preserved in counts(dds)
## estimating dispersions
## fitting model and testing
rna_expression_matrix <- as.matrix(assay(ddsSE_normalized))
rna_expression_transposed <- t(rna_expression_matrix)

1. Hierarchical Clustering

Hierarchical clustering follows a bottom-up approach. It starts with each item as its own cluster and then gradually combines the closest clusters until all items are in a single group. We use Euclidean distance to measure how similar two profiles are. This is a standard way of measuring straight-line distance between points in multi-dimensional space.

# Perform statistical test on each gene
ttest_results_genes <- rowttests(t(rna_expression_matrix))
gene_pvalue_ranking <- order(ttest_results_genes$p.value)

# Select top 30 genes with lowest p-values
top_gene_indices <- gene_pvalue_ranking[1:30]
ranked_gene_matrix <- rna_expression_matrix[top_gene_indices,]

# Calculate Euclidean distance
euclidean_dist_genes <- dist(ranked_gene_matrix)

Gene Clustering

We selected the top 30 most differentially expressed genes by choosing those with the smallest p-values from a statistical test. We calculated the Euclidean distance between the expression profiles of these genes across all samples. We used three different methods to build the dendrograms: Single linkage: joins clusters based on the smallest distance between any two points; Complete linkage: joins clusters based on the largest distance between points; Average linkage: joins clusters based on the average distance between all points. This allowed us to explore how genes group together based on similar expression patterns.

# Complete linkage
cluster_complete <- hclust(euclidean_dist_genes)
plot(cluster_complete, xlab = "", ylab = "Distance", 
     main = "Dendrogram of Top 30 Differentially Expressed Genes\nMethod: Complete Linkage, Euclidean Distance")

# Single linkage
cluster_single <- hclust(euclidean_dist_genes, method = "single")
plot(cluster_single, xlab = "", ylab = "Distance", 
     main = "Dendrogram of Top 30 Differentially Expressed Genes\nMethod: Single Linkage, Euclidean Distance")

# Average linkage
cluster_average <- hclust(euclidean_dist_genes, method = "average")
plot(cluster_average, xlab = "", ylab = "Distance", 
     main = "Dendrogram of Top 30 Differentially Expressed Genes\nMethod: Average Linkage, Euclidean Distance")

# Heatmap of the top 30 genes
# Limit to the 30 most variable genes  
gene_vars <- apply(rna_expression_matrix, 1, var)
top_genes <- names(sort(gene_vars, decreasing = TRUE))[1:30]

# Subset of the matrix with top genes
heatmap_matrix <- rna_expression_matrix[top_genes, ]

# Heatmap with scaling and without column labels (lighter)
heatmap(heatmap_matrix, scale = "row", labCol = FALSE)

The average linkage dendrogram offers the clearest clustering structure among the three, making it the best candidate for further biological interpretation. The heatmap complements the dendrograms and clearly displays expression patterns, which can help identify gene signatures or sample subtypes.

Sample Clustering

We also applied hierarchical clustering to samples (patients). In this case, the matrix was transposed, and distances were calculated between samples using the selected genes. The same linkage methods (single, complete, average) were used to compare how patients cluster. We also created heatmaps to visualize expression patterns and support the dendrogram results.

# Sample-Based Clustering (Hierarchical)

# Use transposed matrix to focus on samples
ttest_results_samples <- rowttests(t(rna_expression_matrix))
sample_pvalue_ranking <- order(ttest_results_samples$p.value)
top_sample_indices <- sample_pvalue_ranking[1:30]

ranked_sample_matrix <- rna_expression_transposed[top_sample_indices,]
euclidean_dist_samples <- dist(ranked_sample_matrix)

# Complete linkage
sample_cluster_complete <- hclust(euclidean_dist_samples)
plot(sample_cluster_complete, xlab = "", ylab = "Distance", 
     main = "Dendrogram of Top 30 Samples\nMethod: Complete Linkage, Euclidean Distance")

# Single linkage
sample_cluster_single <- hclust(euclidean_dist_samples, method = "single")
plot(sample_cluster_single, xlab = "", ylab = "Distance", 
     main = "Dendrogram of Top 30 Samples\nMethod: Single Linkage, Euclidean Distance")

# Average linkage
sample_cluster_average <- hclust(euclidean_dist_samples, method = "average")
plot(sample_cluster_average, xlab = "", ylab = "Distance", 
     main = "Dendrogram of Top 30 Samples\nMethod: Average Linkage, Euclidean Distance")

# Heatmap of the samples
heatmap(ranked_sample_matrix,
        scale = "row",                   # Normalize each gene across samples
        labCol = FALSE,
        col = colorRampPalette(c("blue", "white", "red"))(100))  # More expressive colors

For nearly every gene, the expression values in most samples are below average. There may be very little variation within our selected top 30 samples.

2. K-means Clustering

K-means is a clustering algorithm that divides data into a set number (K) of groups. It does this by placing each data point into the group with the nearest center (centroid), and then adjusting the centers to improve the fit. The goal is to make sure that items in the same group are close to the center and each other.

Finding the Best Number of Clusters

We used the elbow method to find the best number of clusters. The algorithm was run for K = 2 to K = 10. For each K, we calculated the within-cluster sum of squares (WSS) — a measure of how tightly packed the points are inside each cluster. We then plotted WSS vs. K to find the “elbow” point — the spot where increasing K doesn’t improve the result much. This is often a good choice for the number of clusters.

# Determine optimal number of clusters using the elbow method
withinss_values <- c()
for (k in 2:10) {
  kmeans_result <- kmeans(t(rna_expression_matrix), centers = k, nstart = 10)
  withinss_values <- c(withinss_values, kmeans_result$tot.withinss)
}

plot_data <- data.frame(num_clusters = 2:10, wss = withinss_values)

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = num_clusters, y = wss)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Number of Clusters", y = "Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WSS)") +
  theme_minimal()

The WSS decreases as K increases — which is expected, since more clusters naturally reduce the within-group variability. However, the rate of improvement slows down after a certain point. From visual inspection: There’s a noticeable inflection point around K = 4. Beyond that, the WSS reduction is more gradual — suggesting diminishing returns.

Comparing Clusters to Clinical Data

Once we chose a value for K, we ran K-means again to group the samples. We then compared the group assignments with a known clinical variable (vital_status) using a cross-tabulation table.

# K-Means Clustering vs. Clinical Variable

# Use K = 4 clusters (based on elbow plot or prior knowledge)
kmeans_final <- kmeans(t(rna_expression_matrix), centers = 4)
cluster_assignments <- kmeans_final$cluster

# Compare cluster assignments with clinical variable (e.g., vital_status)
comparison_table <- table(cluster_assignments, ddsSE$vital_status)
comparison_table
##                    
## cluster_assignments Alive Dead
##                   1    89   67
##                   2    40   36
##                   3    41   22
##                   4    21    7

This helped us see whether the clusters based on gene expression align with known patient outcomes, possibly revealing meaningful biological differences.

Cluster 1: The largest cluster — contains 223 patients with a nearly balanced but still slightly higher number of Alive (128 vs 95). This might represent a core group with average expression profiles. Cluster 2: Shows 23 Alive vs 14 Dead, suggesting a slightly more favorable survival group. Cluster 3: The smallest cluster — only 22 samples, but fairly balanced (8 vs 14). Cluster 4: Also small, with 26 Alive vs 15 Dead — again, mildly enriched for Alive.

Supervised Analysis

Supervised analysis is a machine learning approach where models are trained using an input dataset along with known labels (outcomes) associated with those data points.
During training, the model learns the relationship between the input features and their labels by iteratively adjusting its internal parameters to minimize the error between its predictions and the true labels.
After training, the model is used to predict the classification or outcome of new, unseen data.

For gene expression data, machine learning models can serve various purposes.
For example, they can predict clinical phenotypes based on gene expression profiles, such as estimating a patient’s response to a particular treatment or predicting disease severity and its progression over time.

Steps for LUAD Gene Expression Data

1. Data Preparation
We first prepare the normalized gene expression data for use in model training and testing.
We set a random seed to make the results reproducible.
We extract the normalized count data from the differential expression analysis object (e.g., dgeObj).
We rank the genes by their p-values from the differential expression analysis, keeping only the significantly differentially expressed genes for machine learning.
This filtering is important because non-differentially expressed genes show little variation and are poor predictors for sample classification.

2. Reshape the Data
Because machine learning models work by classifying samples based on their features (here, genes), we transpose the count matrix so that samples are in the rows and genes are in the columns.

3. Split Into Training and Test Sets
We divide the dataset into ~70% for training and ~30% for testing.
We check that the proportion of outcome classes (e.g., “dead” vs. “alive”) is preserved in both sets to avoid class imbalance, ensuring that no group is over- or under-represented, which helps build more accurate and robust models.

4. Cross-Validation
We set up 10-fold cross-validation to evaluate model performance reliably.
In this setup, the training data is divided into 10 parts (“folds”); in each iteration, one fold is used as validation while the other nine are used for training.
The model is repeatedly trained and evaluated on different combinations of folds.
We configure this setup using the trainControl() function from the caret package.

# Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(42)

# Parameters
top_n_genes <- 100  # Change based on the computational viability
train_frac <- 0.7

# Data preparation
rna_data <- data.frame(dgeObj$counts)
filtered_results_ord <- filtered_results$table[order(filtered_results$table$PValue), ]
de_genes <- rownames(head(filtered_results_ord, top_n_genes))

# Create combined dataset 
rna_data_vital_status <- data.frame(
  vital = factor(expression_filtered$vital_status), 
  t(rna_data)[, de_genes, drop = FALSE]
)

# Ensure valid factor levels for modeling
levels(rna_data_vital_status$vital) <- make.names(levels(rna_data_vital_status$vital))

# Data validation
stopifnot(!any(is.na(rna_data_vital_status)))
stopifnot(all(de_genes %in% colnames(rna_data_vital_status)))

# Split data
train_idx <- createDataPartition(rna_data_vital_status$vital, p = train_frac, list = FALSE)
train_set <- rna_data_vital_status[train_idx, ]
test_set <- rna_data_vital_status[-train_idx, ]

# Check dimensions of the splits
cat("Training set dimensions:", dim(train_set), "\n")
## Training set dimensions: 227 101
cat("Test set dimensions:", dim(test_set), "\n")
## Test set dimensions: 96 101
# Check class balance
cat("\nClass proportions:\n")
## 
## Class proportions:
cat("- Full dataset:\n")
## - Full dataset:
print(prop.table(table(rna_data_vital_status$vital)))
## 
##     Alive      Dead 
## 0.5913313 0.4086687
cat("\n- Training set:\n")
## 
## - Training set:
print(prop.table(table(train_set$vital)))
## 
##     Alive      Dead 
## 0.5903084 0.4096916
cat("\n- Test set:\n")
## 
## - Test set:
print(prop.table(table(test_set$vital)))
## 
##   Alive    Dead 
## 0.59375 0.40625
# Create 10 cross-validation folds, stratified by class
folds <- createFolds(train_set$vital, k = 10, list = TRUE)

# Set up training control with correct fold indices
cv_control <- trainControl(
  method = "cv",
  number = 10,
  index = folds,
  savePredictions = "final",
  classProbs = TRUE,
  summaryFunction = twoClassSummary,  # Add if doing binary classification
  verboseIter = TRUE  # Recommended to see progress
)
# List of models to compare with tuning parameters
models <- list(
  rf = list(method = "rf", tuneLength = 5),
  svmRadial = list(method = "svmRadial", tuneLength = 5),
  glm = list(method = "glm"),
  knn = list(method = "knn", tuneLength = 10)
)

# Store results
model_list <- list()

# Train each model
for (m in names(models)) {
  set.seed(42)
  cat("Training:", m, "\n")
  
  # Create specific arguments list
  args <- list(
    x = train_set[, -which(names(train_set) == "vital")],  # predictors
    y = train_set$vital,                                  # outcome
    method = models[[m]]$method,
    trControl = cv_control,
    preProcess = c("center", "scale")
  )
  
  # Add model-specific arguments
  if (!is.null(models[[m]]$tuneLength)) {
    args$tuneLength <- models[[m]]$tuneLength
  }
  if (m == "glm") {
    args$family <- binomial()  # Note: binomial() function, not string
  }
  
  model_list[[m]] <- do.call(train, args)
}

# Compare models
resamps <- resamples(model_list)

# Summary metrics
summary(resamps)

# Visual comparison
dotplot(resamps, metric = "ROC")  # Or "Accuracy"/other metrics

# Identify best model (based on ROC)
perf_metrics <- sapply(model_list, function(x) max(x$results$ROC, na.rm = TRUE))
best_model_name <- names(which.max(perf_metrics))
best_model <- model_list[[best_model_name]]

cat("\nBest model is:", best_model_name, "with ROC of", max(perf_metrics), "\n")
## 
## Best model is: knn with ROC of 0.5426161
# Evaluate on test set
test_pred <- predict(best_model, newdata = test_set)  # Consistent naming
conf_mat <- confusionMatrix(test_pred, test_set$vital, positive = levels(test_set$vital)[2])
print(conf_mat)
## Confusion Matrix and Statistics
## 
##           Reference
## Prediction Alive Dead
##      Alive    39   24
##      Dead     18   15
##                                           
##                Accuracy : 0.5625          
##                  95% CI : (0.4575, 0.6636)
##     No Information Rate : 0.5938          
##     P-Value [Acc > NIR] : 0.7673          
##                                           
##                   Kappa : 0.0705          
##                                           
##  Mcnemar's Test P-Value : 0.4404          
##                                           
##             Sensitivity : 0.3846          
##             Specificity : 0.6842          
##          Pos Pred Value : 0.4545          
##          Neg Pred Value : 0.6190          
##              Prevalence : 0.4062          
##          Detection Rate : 0.1562          
##    Detection Prevalence : 0.3438          
##       Balanced Accuracy : 0.5344          
##                                           
##        'Positive' Class : Dead            
## 
# ROC analysis
if(nlevels(test_set$vital) == 2) {  # Only for binary classification
  test_prob <- predict(best_model, newdata = test_set, type = "prob")[, 2]
  roc_obj <- roc(response = test_set$vital, predictor = test_prob)
  plot(roc_obj, print.auc = TRUE)
  cat("AUC on test set:", auc(roc_obj), "\n")
}
## Setting levels: control = Alive, case = Dead
## Setting direction: controls < cases

## AUC on test set: 0.5537562
